thread.title: CDC Director Susan Monarez Departs Weeks Into Role

author: Ethan Brooks
title: CDC Director Susan Monarez Departs Weeks Into Role
text:
ATLANTA, Aug. 28, 2025 — Susan Monarez, the long-serving federal scientist recently confirmed as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), is out of her role just weeks after taking the helm. The Department of Health and Human Services confirmed Monarez’s departure Wednesday evening.
### Monarez Ousted Amid Vaccine Policy Clash
The agency stated on X that “Susan Monarez is no longer director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. We thank her for her dedicated service to the American people.” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy reportedly pushed for Monarez’s resignation.
The department offered no specific reason for her exit, and an immediate request for comment from the agency went unanswered.
Reports suggest the departure stemmed from Monarez’s hesitation to fully support the administration’s evolving coronavirus vaccine policies without consulting her advisers. Sources familiar with the discussions indicated Monarez’s refusal to commit immediately, followed by an attempt to seek support from Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, further angered Kennedy. Monarez, who declined to resign immediately, was subsequently instructed to step down or face termination.
Under Kennedy’s leadership, who is noted as a vaccine skeptic, the HHS has been actively shifting national vaccine policies. On Wednesday, the FDA approved new COVID-19 shot restrictions, limiting eligibility to high-risk groups. Earlier in August, HHS announced a winding down of mRNA vaccine development at an agency focused on public health emergencies, despite the vaccines’ credited role in saving millions of lives during the pandemic.
### Top Officials Resign in Wake of Departure
At least three senior CDC officials have resigned following Monarez’s exit. Among them were Daniel Jernigan, director of the National Center for Emerging Zoonotic Infectious Diseases; Chief Medical Officer Deb Houry; and Demetre Daskalakis, director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases.
Daskalakis cited “the ongoing weaponization of public health” as his reason for leaving. Houry expressed commitment to public health but stated that “ongoing changes prevent me from continuing in my job as a leader of the agency,” adding that science should “never be censored or subject to political interpretations.”
Monarez, the first CDC director confirmed by the Senate and the only non-physician to lead the agency, was sworn in on July 31. At the time, Kennedy lauded her as “a public health expert with unimpeachable scientific credentials.” He expressed full confidence in her ability to restore the CDC’s standing and strengthen the nation’s preparedness for infectious diseases and biosecurity threats. Prior to her directorship, Monarez served as Acting Director and Deputy Director for the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health.
Her departure occurs shortly after a shooting incident on the CDC’s Atlanta campus on August 8, which resulted in the death of DeKalb County police officer David Rose.
Monarez’s swift exit echoes previous rapid departures of Trump administration officials. Billy Long was removed as Internal Revenue Service chief just two months after his confirmation earlier this month. These recent events are reminiscent of brief tenures during President Trump’s first term, such as Anthony Scaramucci’s 10-day stint as White House Communications Director and Mike Flynn’s 24-day tenure as National Security Advisor in 2017.
Susan Monarez, confirmed as CDC director in late July, has departed the agency after only a few weeks. The Department of Health and Human Services confirmed her exit, with reports suggesting a clash over vaccine policy with Secretary Robert F. Kennedy. Three high-ranking officials resigned from the CDC following Monarez’s departure, citing concerns over the “weaponization of public health.” Monarez’s tenure was marked by shifts in vaccine policy and occurred shortly after a shooting incident at the CDC’s Atlanta campus.
